extracted.intended_audience: students of literature, literary critics, and aspiring poets/readers of Romantic-era English poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative criteria and standards used in Hazlitt's lectures for judging poets and poetic works (style, authenticity, imagination vs. reason, novelty, etc.). Aimed at assessing/teaching poetic quality in English Romantic and 18th–19th-century contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluency and elegance of verse
rubrics_metrics.description: 'most flowing and elegant of our versifiers' — verse should have ease, flow, and an elegant manner of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Goldsmith as 'the most flowing and elegant of our versifiers since Pope,' adding that this quality often pairs with 'traits of artless nature' and a 'peculiar felicity in his turns upon words,' sometimes repeating phrases 'with delightful effect.' Anti-patterns: stiff, laboured, or overly ornate diction that obstructs natural flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artless/natural grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should show 'artless' or unstudied manners—grace that feels spontaneous rather than forced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goldsmith is lauded for 'careless inimitable grace' and 'manners unstudied, but a gentle heart'—learning and skill should appear subordinate to natural ease. Guidance: prefer simplicity and unaffected charm over finical artistry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Felicity in turns of phrase and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Skillful turns upon words and tasteful repetition that produce a delightful effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Goldsmith's repeated phrases ('He sees that little lot, the lot of all') are noted for felicity. Repetition should enhance effect rather than feel monotonous or merely rhetorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality combined with tasteful imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A good poet can work from a model yet adorn and improve what is copied; originality need not be absolute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt: 'His genius was a mixture of originality and imitation: he could do nothing without some model before him, and he could copy nothing that he did not adorn with the graces of his own mind.' Scoring note: value both imaginative originality and the ability to transform sources gracefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelistic charm through domestic incident and comic detail
rubrics_metrics.description: In prose (novels), charm can arise from vivid domestic anecdotes and comic situations grounded in everyday life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goldsmith's Vicar of Wakefield is praised for episodes (the poker, the unchanged guinea, painted Flamborough family) that enliven narrative. Guidance: rich, concrete incidents and comic detail increase reader delight; avoid abstract or remote anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic characterisation suited to performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic writing should create characters that 'draw forth new powers' in performance—distinctive, stage-able traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Tony Lumpkin 'draws forth new powers from Mr. Liston's face.' Criterion useful for dramatic/comic writing: characters should register vividly in performance and embody comic types rather than generic sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and suitability of form (e.g., sonnet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short forms like the sonnet have the 'necessary advantage of being short' and should treat pleasing subjects in a pleasing, concentrated way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes sonnets' advantage of brevity, but cautions they can be 'both tedious and brief.' Use the form's concision to focus and heighten thought; avoid undue prolixity or emptiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning should serve interesting thought, not pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarship and learning are valuable only insofar as they lead to interesting thought and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Warton's sonnets: 'Nothing can be more admirable than the learning here displayed, or the inference from it, that it is of no use but as it leads to interesting thought and reflection.' Anti-pattern: pedantic display of facts that don't illuminate feeling or idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge works by their intrinsic excellence, not by circumstances of production
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate poems and authors by the quality of their works rather than by the novelty of their circumstances (e.g., an author's youth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt criticises estimations of Chatterton based on 'prematureness' rather than on lasting excellence: 'the side-mark of the age... wears out in works destined for immortality.' Scoring note: discount extrinsic curiosities (age, misfortune) when assessing merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude in historical or archaic pastiche
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitations of earlier styles must be convincing in both language and pronunciation; inconsistencies betray an imposture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt argues the Rowley-forgery fails because 'the poems read as smooth as any modern poems, if you read them as modern compositions' and because obsolete spellings mismatch modern pronunciation. Anti-pattern: forced archaisms and inconsistent linguistic choices that break plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of imagination: privileging immediate impression and emotional extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's office is to 'pamper the imagination' and to insist on immediate impressions—evoking ecstasy or agony rather than coolly estimating consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt contrasts imagination and reason: imagination indulges immediate impressions and the extremes of feeling; poets may rightly aim for vivid, intense moments rather than prosaic balance. Evaluation: does the poem successfully produce those immediate impressions?

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity derived from lived experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Credible depiction of certain subjects (e.g., convivial excess, drinking, local customs) depends on the poet's experiential knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt argues Burns could write Tam o'Shanter because he had lived the habits portrayed; Wordsworth could not have written it 'without any knowledge of them.' Anti-pattern: claiming verisimilitude while lacking experiential grounding, which can produce inauthentic or unconvincing representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete, natural imagery over artificial diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer imagery drawn from common, natural life (e.g., 'mountain-daisy') rather than 'artificial flowers' or contrived poetic ornament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Burns for 'plucked the mountain-daisy under his feet' instead of relying on contrived imagery. Guidance: concrete particulars make feeling believable and vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robustness and sincerity of feeling (avoid sickly sentimentality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should exhibit manliness, vigor, and unfeigned feeling rather than sickly sentimentality or 'namby-pamby' affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt: Burns 'was not a sickly sentimentalist... He was as much of a man'—valuing frankness, strength, and honest emotion. Anti-patterns: excessive mawkishness, sentimental posturing that lacks assertive feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to depict social life, humour, and manners vividly
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong poet can render social fellowship, jocularity, and local manners with vividness and truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Burns's 'pictures of good fellowship, of social glee, of quaint humour' 'come up to nature.' Evaluation checks for authenticity of social scenes, comic detail, and sympathy toward common life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate moral judgment of the person from artistic appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical assessment should distinguish the poet's private morals from the poetic merits of their works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt defends evaluating Burns' poetry despite attacks on his moral character; he criticises conflating moral reproach with literary judgment. Scoring note: moral censure may inform context but should not automatically devalue artistic achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and breadth of appeal as an evaluative dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet's taste—whether exclusive or widely sympathetic—affects how many readers he pleases; exclusiveness may limit audience though not necessarily quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt notes Wordsworth's taste 'gives pleasure to so few people' because it is exclusive; evaluation should note intended audience and accessibility as part of quality assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid depiction of local customs and scenery
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective poetry often captures local customs, scenery, and vernacular detail, lending picturesqueness and specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt praises Burns' 'Halloween' and 'Brigs of Ayr' for striking and picturesque description of local customs. Guidance: look for sensory, scene-based detail that situates the poem culturally and geographically.
